summary: This Informational document describes the AEGIS-128L, AEGIS-256, AEGIS-128X, and AEGIS-256X authenticated encryption algorithms, which are AES-based and designed for high performance. It also covers their use as stream ciphers and message authentication codes. It is a product of the CFRG.

plainLanguage.summary: A family of fast secret-code recipes that both scramble a message and prove nobody changed it.

questions: aead based on aes high performance
subtitle: Fast authenticated encryption algorithms built from the AES round function.

tldr.problem: Widely-deployed authenticated encryption schemes like AES-GCM, while secure, do not achieve optimal performance on modern processors with AES acceleration, and they have limitations on nonce reuse with random nonces.
tldr.mechanism: AEGIS is a family of four AES-based authenticated encryption algorithms (AEGIS-128L, AEGIS-256, AEGIS-128X, AEGIS-256X) designed for high performance. They use only the AES round function, not its inverse, and provide both regular and parallelizable modes for different hardware capabilities.
tldr.outcome: AEGIS offers significantly faster performance than AES-GCM, provides better nonce-reuse safety (especially AEGIS-256), resists certain attacks like partitioning oracle attacks, and can erase keys early without affecting security.

today: RFC 10032, published in September 2026, is an Informational RFC representing the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG), an IRTF working group. It documents AEGIS designs that may be suitable for high-performance cryptography, though IRTF informational documents are not candidates for Internet Standard status. AEGIS is already implemented in several cryptographic libraries and shows promise for deployment in performance-critical applications.

sections.title: Purpose and Performance
sections.content:
AEGIS is a family of authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) algorithms that were finalists in the CAESAR (Competition for Authenticated Encryption: Security, Applicability, and Robustness) competition, which sought ciphers optimized for high-performance applications. While AEGIS-128 won the competition, RFC 10032 documents AEGIS-128L (another finalist offering better performance and security margin) and AEGIS-256 (which reached the finals and provides 256-bit security).

The key advantage of AEGIS is performance. It significantly exceeds AES-GCM on CPUs with AES instructions, and software implementations are faster even without hardware acceleration. Unlike AES-GCM, AEGIS-128L can safely encrypt up to 2^48 messages with random nonces before collision becomes likely, and AEGIS-256 allows random nonces with no practical limits. All variants are built only from the AES round function, not the full AES encryption, making them efficient to implement.
sections.plainLanguage: AEGIS is much faster than older encryption methods when your computer has built-in encryption support. It also lets you use random keys much more safely, which is important for security.

sections.title: Four Algorithm Variants
sections.content:
RFC 10032 specifies four AEGIS variants, organized into two families based on key size. AEGIS-128L has a 128-bit key and nonce, a 1024-bit internal state, and processes 256-bit input blocks. AEGIS-256 has a 256-bit key and nonce, a 768-bit internal state, and processes 128-bit blocks. Both can produce 128-bit or 256-bit authentication tags.

The other two variants are parallel modes optimized for modern processors with large vector registers and vector AES instructions. AEGIS-128X is based on AEGIS-128L but processes multiple independent instances in parallel (hence the "X"; the RFC covers AEGIS-128X2 and AEGIS-128X4). AEGIS-256X is the parallel variant of AEGIS-256. These parallel modes offer even higher throughput on capable hardware while maintaining the same security and key/nonce properties as their base algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four recipes: two main ones (AEGIS-128L and AEGIS-256) that differ in key size, and two turbo versions (with X) that run faster by doing multiple encryptions at once on powerful computers.

sections.title: How AEGIS Works
sections.content:
AEGIS is inverse-free, meaning it uses only the AES encryption round function, not the AES decryption function. This is unusual: most cipher modes use both encryption and decryption, but AEGIS needs only one direction. The algorithm processes data through an initialization phase that mixes the key and nonce into an internal state, then repeatedly updates the state with plaintext and associated data, encrypts data, and finally produces an authentication tag.

A critical security property is that leaking the internal state does not compromise the key or past states—the key is only needed during initialization. After initialization completes, the key can be securely erased from memory. This matters for defending against cold-boot attacks, where an attacker with physical access tries to read cryptographic keys from RAM. Additionally, AEGIS provides committing security: an attacker trying to forge a ciphertext that validates under multiple keys faces ~2^64 attempts with a 128-bit tag (generally acceptable for interactive protocols) or ~2^128 attempts with a 256-bit tag (impractical).
sections.plainLanguage: AEGIS keeps the message and proof number completely separate, so if someone steals the internal working memory, they can't steal your encryption key. It also makes it extremely hard for bad guys to trick the system into accepting a fake message under the wrong key.

sections.title: Security and Usage
sections.content:
AEGIS has specific requirements for safe use. A nonce must never be used twice with the same key, or the plaintext differences are immediately revealed. Every key must be chosen randomly. The nonce itself can be public or predictable (a counter, permutation output, or long-period generator), which is more flexible than some schemes.

AEGIS resists partitioning oracle attacks, where attackers craft ciphertexts that decrypt under multiple keys. With AES-GCM, this attack reduces password guessing from brute-force to binary search—dangerously practical. With AEGIS, the same attack requires ~2^64 or ~2^128 attempts depending on tag size, making it impractical. Unlike most AES-based constructions, there is no key schedule that could leak information, and the key can be erased immediately after initialization without affecting security. AEGIS-256 and AEGIS-256X can safely use random nonces without worrying about birthday-bound collisions; AEGIS-128L and AEGIS-128X have a much larger safe range than AES-GCM (2^48 messages vs. roughly 2^32).
sections.plainLanguage: Use a different random number with each message, or the attacker sees what changed. AEGIS makes it incredibly hard to guess passwords by trying many of them at once. And you can forget the encryption key right after you set it up, which makes the system harder to hack.

sections.title: Stream Ciphers and Message Authentication
sections.content:
AEGIS can also function as a stream cipher, generating a pseudorandom keystream from the key and nonce. The plaintext is XORed with this keystream to produce ciphertext. This mode provides confidentiality but not authentication by itself.

Additionally, RFC 10032 defines message authentication code (MAC) variants: AEGISMAC-128L, AEGISMAC-256, AEGISMAC-128X, and AEGISMAC-256X. These variants produce an authentication tag over data without encrypting it, allowing you to verify message integrity and authenticity. The RFC includes comprehensive test vectors for all variants, enabling consistent implementation across different libraries and systems. All variants use the same key-nonce handling requirements and share the same security properties with respect to committing security and key erasure.
sections.plainLanguage: AEGIS can also work as just a scrambler without proof numbers, or as just a proof number without scrambling. This makes it flexible for different use cases.
